prompt:

Reply with ONLY one JSON object:

   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))

 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?

   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Johnson Controls fits few Rule Breaker traits: it is a 140-year-old company in a mature industry, not the top dog of a new one, though it is a leading supplier of cooling for the fast-growing AI data-center market. The shares rose about 30.6% over 52 weeks to $147.50 (Oct 26, 2026), well ahead of the S&P 500, but the business lacks a consumer brand or a hard-to-copy innovation edge.
summaries.buffett: JCI is an understandable equipment-plus-service business with a long dividend record (paid since 1887), but its moat is moderate against Trane, Carrier and Daikin, returns on capital are middling (ROIC about 12.8%) and earnings have been uneven, including a FY2016 loss after the Tyco merger. At about 29 times FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance, it offers no margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Inverting, the main ways JCI could disappoint are a pause in AI data-center building, a shift to liquid cooling that bypasses large chillers, AFFF litigation and execution slips in its new business system. The business is decent but not exceptional, and the price (about 25 times trailing earnings) already assumes the turnaround works.
summaries.lynch: Lynch would class JCI as a turnaround-plus-stalwart: a refocused commercial HVAC company with a clear story of data-center demand and Danaher-style margin gains (adjusted EPS guided to about $5.05 for FY2026, up about 34% from $3.76). The P/E of about 29 on FY2026 guidance is below this year's growth, but next year's expected EPS growth (about 18%) is lower and part of the gain comes from the $5 billion buyback.
summaries.fisher: JCI scores moderately on Fisher's points: it is adding new products as markets shift (coolant distribution units with a pipeline above $1 billion, an absorption-chiller reference design for AI factories) and a large service force sells into a growing installed base. Weaknesses are an R&D record that has not created a clear technology lead and a management team that has been in place only since 2025.
summaries.graham: JCI fails most of Graham's defensive tests: it pays a dividend unbroken since 1887 and is large, but it lost money in FY2016, trades at about 25 times trailing earnings and 6.6 times book (a product near 169 versus Graham's 22.5 limit), and its current ratio is only about 1.0.
summaries.thiel: JCI is not a Zero-to-One business: it has no proprietary technology ten times better than rivals and competes in a crowded market with Trane, Carrier, Daikin, Siemens and Honeywell. Its strengths are distribution and service reach, plus good timing in data-center cooling, which Thiel would see as incremental rather than monopoly-building.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner would like the operating leverage story (FY2026 operating leverage guided at 45-50%, orders up 27% organically in Q3) and the AI infrastructure exposure, but the stock already trades at about 25 times forward earnings with low free-cash-flow yield, so the reward depends on continued estimate increases.
summaries.druckenmiller: The setup has Druckenmiller-style momentum: earnings are accelerating, FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance has been raised three times from about $4.55 to about $5.05, the stock is up about 30.6% in a year and AI data-center spending is a strong tailwind. The main risks are a turn in the data-center capex cycle and a full valuation.
summaries.smith: Terry Smith would see a reasonable but not outstanding business: gross margin about 36%, ROIC about 12.8% and heavy restructuring charges fall short of his high-return, low-capital-intensity ideal. At about 25 times earnings and under a 4% free-cash-flow yield, he would also find the price too full for the quality.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula, JCI ranks poorly: its earnings yield is low (EV/EBIT about 27.7, or about 3.6%) and its return on capital is middling, so it would not appear near the top of a screen.
summaries.akre: On Akre's three-legged stool, JCI's business quality is moderate, management (CEO Joakim Weidemanis since March 2025, ex-Danaher) looks capable but is new, and reinvestment opportunities in data-center cooling are good; the high valuation and only average returns on capital make it a weak fit.
summaries.pabrai: JCI is not a Dhandho bet: there is no distressed price, the downside is not tightly limited at about 25 times earnings, and the upside depends on a data-center boom the market already recognizes.
summaries.wood: JCI is not a Cathie Wood company: it is an established equipment maker benefiting indirectly from AI infrastructure, not a leader in an innovation platform with falling cost curves.
summaries.ackman: JCI partly fits Ackman's criteria: a simple, predictable, mostly North American commercial building-systems business with a moderate moat, a new CEO improving operations and big buybacks. Its leverage, cyclical exposure to construction and moderate returns on capital fall short of his preference for dominant, high-return franchises.
summaries.sleep: JCI does not show Nick Sleep's scale-economies-shared model: it does not pass savings back to customers in a way that compounds its advantage, and its position in 10-20 years is not clearly stronger than rivals'.
summaries.valentine: Valentine looked for huge markets and technology shifts; JCI is a mature industrial selling into a large, growing market (AI data centers, decarbonization), but it is not a startup with a new technology, so his framework applies only loosely.
summaries.nash: Under Tom Nash's process JCI rides a real secular trend (AI data-center cooling) and is a large, profitable, widely owned company that beat earnings estimates in each of the last four quarters. It fails several key filters: more debt than cash ($9,475M vs $641M), revenue growth below 10%, operating margin below 20%, a CEO with little tenure or open-market buying, and a DCF value well below the $147.50 price.

momentum.evidence: JCI rose about 30.6% over 52 weeks to $147.50 on Oct 26, 2026 (StockAnalysis), against a one-year total return of about 14.2% for the S&P 500 ETF SPY, though it has been roughly flat since April 2026.

g4.evidence: CEO Joakim Weidemanis ran Danaher's Diagnostics and China businesses and is installing a Danaher-style business system, and institutions own about 92% of shares, but there is no famous anchor investor.

g6.evidence: Some brokers (Mizuho, RBC) rate it Hold at $150-165 targets close to the price, but most analysts (BofA $175, Morgan Stanley $180, Bernstein $190) rate it Buy, so it is not widely called overvalued.

simple.evidence: It sells and services HVAC equipment, building controls and fire and security systems for large buildings, a business a generalist can understand.

b2.evidence: It has paid a dividend every year since 1887, but earnings have swung with the 2016 Tyco merger (FY2016 loss of $868M), restructuring and portfolio sales.

integrity.evidence: Disclosure is clear and governance conventional (PwC auditor, 18 years on Ethisphere's ethics list), but CEO pay is large ($1.5M salary plus $12M FY2026 long-term awards) and insiders own only about 0.2%.

b6.evidence: The new management is shrinking rather than empire-building, having sold residential HVAC to Bosch and returned $5,991M through buybacks in FY2025, but past management built the company through the large Tyco merger.

roic.evidence: ROIC is about 12.8% (StockAnalysis) with debt to equity of about 0.70, decent but not high, and returns have been diluted by goodwill of $16,612M from past deals.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow was $2,120M (adjusted $2,501M) against $1,721M of continuing income, and management guides about 100% adjusted FCF conversion, but trailing FCF of $1.66B was depressed by taxes on the Bosch sale.

b10.evidence: The share price roughly doubled over five years (from about $73 in Oct 2021 to $147.50), but much of the retained money went to the Tyco merger and restructuring charges that created little value for many years.

safety.evidence: At about 25 times trailing earnings and 22.7 times EV/EBITDA, the price is above a conservative estimate of value, with no margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 29 times FY2026 adjusted EPS guidance of $5.05 and about 25 times FY2027 estimates is a full price for a business growing sales about 8% organically, though EPS is growing faster.

mu5.evidence: A large installed base and service business make outright failure unlikely, but a data-center capex slowdown, liquid-cooling disruption and AFFF litigation are real risks.

reinvest.evidence: Data-center cooling and liquid cooling offer reinvestment room (backlog $21.0B, up 32% organically), but returns on capital of about 12.8% are only moderate.

ly2.evidence: It is a clear turnaround/stalwart: a refocused commercial building-systems company where data-center demand and a new business system lift margins and EPS.

ly3.evidence: The P/E of about 29 on FY2026 guidance is below this year's roughly 34% adjusted EPS growth, but above the roughly 18% growth analysts expect for FY2027 (MarketScreener EPS about $5.98).

runway.evidence: Analysts expect revenue to grow about 8% a year to about $29.7B by FY2028, and the CFO sees data centers reaching about one-third of revenue in 3-5 years, but core building markets grow more slowly.

ly7.evidence: The company cut its diluted share count from 753.6M (FY2020) to about 610M (Q3 FY2026), including a $5.0B accelerated buyback, but no insider open-market buying was found.

ly8.evidence: JCI is an S&P 500 company with a market value of about $89B, about 92% institutional ownership and over 20 analysts covering it.

fi2.evidence: It is launching new products for new demand, including coolant distribution units (pipeline above $1 billion, shipments starting in Q4 FY2026) and an absorption-chiller design that could cut AI-factory cooling power by about 44%.

fi3.evidence: Development work is producing data-center products and a 40% faster time to market on one product, but JCI does not hold a clear technology lead over Trane or Vertiv.

fi4.evidence: Orders rose 27% organically in Q3 FY2026 through a large direct sales and service force, but this mostly reflects market demand rather than unusual selling skill.

longterm.evidence: Management is investing in a long-term business system and new data-center products, while also prioritizing near-term EPS guidance and large buybacks.

gr1.evidence: It had $23,596M of FY2025 sales and a market value of about $89B.

ni10.evidence: It reported a net loss attributable of $868M in FY2016 after the Tyco merger, within the last ten fiscal years.

gr4.evidence: Johnson Controls says it has paid a consecutive dividend since 1887, most recently $0.40 per share paid Oct 16, 2026.

eps10.evidence: Total diluted EPS rose from $2.36 (FY2015) to $5.03 (FY2025), but FY2025 includes the gain on the residential HVAC sale; continuing-operations EPS of $2.63 is only about 11% above FY2015's $2.36.

gr6.evidence: The price of $147.50 is about 25 times trailing earnings and far above 15 times average earnings.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 25.5 times P/B of about 6.6 gives about 169, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Its chillers, controls and fire systems are competitive but not ten times better than Trane, Carrier, Daikin or Siemens.

timing.evidence: AI data-center construction is driving record demand for cooling, with Americas orders up 37% and backlog up 32% organically in Q3 FY2026.

th3.evidence: JCI did not start with a dominant share of a small market; it is an incumbent with a modest share of large, competitive markets.

team.evidence: Weidemanis brings a strong Danaher operating record, but he has led JCI only since March 2025 and is not a founder.

th5.evidence: It has a large direct sales and service network reaching building owners worldwide, with services 31.7% of FY2025 sales.

durable.evidence: Buildings will still need cooling, controls and fire safety in 10-20 years and JCI's installed base is sticky, but liquid cooling and software could shift value to other players.

th7.evidence: Data-center cooling demand is widely recognized, and Trane, Vertiv, Schneider and Carrier are pursuing the same opportunity.

trend.evidence: JCI is a meaningful AI data-center beneficiary (expected high-teens percent of FY2026 revenue), but Vertiv, Trane and Schneider are equal or larger beneficiaries.

dr1.evidence: Adjusted EPS rose about 45% in Q2 and 35% in Q3 FY2026, and FY2026 guidance was raised from about $4.55 to $4.70, $4.85 and then $5.05.

dr2.evidence: A $21.0B backlog and the business system should lift results over 18-24 months, but this improvement is already widely expected and reflected in a 25x forward P/E.

dr4.evidence: Lower rates would help commercial construction and data-center financing, but EMEA growth was only 1% organic in Q3 FY2026 because of Middle East conflicts.

dr6.evidence: Upcoming catalysts include Q4 FY2026 results and FY2027 guidance in November 2026, first coolant-distribution-unit shipments and continued data-center orders.

dr7.evidence: With a moderate moat, full valuation and data-center cycle risk, conviction is not high enough for a large concentrated position.

gm.evidence: Gross margin of 36.4% in FY2025 (36.65% trailing) is solid for industrial equipment but not high.

fcfyield.evidence: Trailing FCF yield is about 1.9%, and even on FY2026 estimated FCF of about $3.05B (MarketScreener) it is only about 3.4% of the $89B market value.

gb2.evidence: EV/EBIT of about 27.7 means operating profit is only about 3.6% of enterprise value.

pa2.evidence: The business is not in a setback; orders, backlog and EPS guidance are at record levels.

pa4.evidence: The installed base and service revenue limit business risk, but a high multiple means a de-rating could cause a large, lasting share-price loss.

wo1.evidence: JCI supplies cooling to AI data centers but is not a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomics.

wo2.evidence: HVAC and fire equipment costs are not falling rapidly with volume in a way that unlocks large new demand.

wo3.evidence: It does not combine several innovation platforms; it is a building-systems company with an AI-related end market.

wo4.evidence: Its addressable market grows mid- to high-single digits, not many times larger in five years.

ac3.evidence: Services (31.7% of sales) are steady, but equipment demand depends on construction, interest rates and copper and steel costs.

ns1.evidence: There is no evidence JCI passes scale savings to customers to widen its lead; it is focused on raising margins.

ns4.evidence: Data-center exposure and the business system could strengthen it, but it is not clearly positioned to be stronger relative to rivals in 10-20 years.

va2.evidence: Keeping data centers, hospitals and other critical buildings cooled and fire-safe is a large and painful problem for owners.

tn1.evidence: It sells into the AI data-center trend at the cooling infrastructure layer, but it is an old building-systems business retrofitting to that trend rather than built for it.

tn2.evidence: The market still often sees JCI as a slow conglomerate, while it is becoming a focused thermal-management company with data centers heading toward about one-third of revenue, though analysts already highlight this.

tn3.evidence: It is a large-cap, Irish-domiciled industrial with mainly U.S. operations, outside the small-cap, Chinese, commodity, airline, seasonal and startup zones.

tn4.evidence: It passes two of three: sales grew every year from FY2022 to FY2025 and it is profitable, but debt ($9,475M) far exceeds cash ($641M).

tn5.evidence: Free cash flow has been positive (Q3 FY2026 $1,194M), but cash has been far below debt every recent quarter (June 30, 2026: $641M vs $9,475M).

tn6.evidence: Sales grew 2.8% in FY2025 and nine-month FY2026 sales rose about 8.2%, below 10% a year.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about 8% plus a trailing FCF margin of about 6.6% is about 15, far below 40.

tn8.evidence: Management reports 45-50% operating leverage in FY2026, and segment margins rose 110-260 basis points in Q3, showing revenue growing faster than expenses.

tn9.evidence: It hits instant kills: more debt than cash and an operating margin of about 14.2%, below 20%.

tn10.evidence: Its former Tyco Fire Products unit faces ongoing AFFF firefighting-foam litigation, though it is not an existential threat.

tn11.evidence: JCI provides cooling, controls and fire and security systems that help building and data-center owners run safe, efficient facilities, and charges for equipment plus recurring service contracts.

tn13.evidence: Total 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5 (14.2%), short interest 10 (1.5%), institutional ownership 10 (92%), revenue faster than expenses 10, 5-year return vs S&P 500 10 (about +121% total return vs roughly +75%), moat 5, CEO 5, pricing power 0 (cyclical construction exposure), secular trend 5, culture and mission 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Cash was below debt every year and operating results swung with restructuring charges, so not every test was met despite rising sales.

tn15.evidence: Interest coverage is about 17x, the current ratio is about 1.0 and liabilities are about 1.9 times equity, but assets excluding goodwill ($22,147M) are only about 0.9 times liabilities ($25,244M).

tn18.evidence: Weidemanis has led JCI only since March 2025, is not a founder and no open-market share purchases by him were found.

tn20.evidence: JCI beat earnings expectations in each of the last four quarters (Q4 FY2025 to Q3 FY2026), e.g. Q2 adjusted EPS of $1.19 vs a $1.12 Zacks consensus and Q3 $1.42 vs guidance of about $1.28.

tn21.evidence: No clown CEO, co-CEO, acquisition spree, auditor change (PwC) or accounting concerns were found, margins are rising, and no heavy insider selling was reported.

tn22.evidence: It has $23.6B of revenue, profits, buybacks rather than share sales and no media hype.

tn24.evidence: At about 3.4% forward FCF yield, the price implies long-term growth above the roughly 8% organic sales growth JCI is delivering.

tn25.evidence: Using a 3-year average revenue growth of about 4.6% and FCF margin of about 6.7%, a 12% discount rate and 4% terminal growth, minus about $8.8B net debt, gives roughly $20 a share, far below $147.50.

tn26.evidence: Forward P/E of about 25 with a PEG of about 1.14 (StockAnalysis) is above 1, and in line with or above peers rather than attractive.
